The CDC, along with its planners and content experts, has disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. 2. This report will not discuss the unlabeled use of a product or investigational use of a product, except for the off-label use of the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) in specific situations. 3. The interval between the administration of Td and Tdap may be shorter than the five years indicated in the package insert. 4. Progressive neurological disorders are not considered a contraindication for Tdap as indicated in the package insert, but unstable neurological disorders (e.g., cerebrovascular events, acute encephalopathic conditions) are considered precautions and may warrant deferral of Tdap and/or Td administration. 5. Tdap can be used as part of the primary vaccination series for tetanus and diphtheria. 6. The inadvertent administration of Tdap and pediatric DTaP is discussed. 7. Pertussis is an acute, infectious respiratory illness that remains endemic in the United States despite routine childhood vaccination programs. 8. Immunity to pertussis wanes approximately 5–10 years after completing childhood vaccination, leaving adolescents and adults susceptible to infection. 9. Since the 1980s, the number of reported pertussis cases has steadily increased, particularly among adolescents and adults. 10. In 2005, a total of 25,616 cases of pertussis were reported in the United States. 11. Among vaccine-preventable bacterial diseases for which universal childhood vaccination is recommended, pertussis is the least well-controlled in the United States. 12. In 2005, a Tdap vaccine formulated for use in adolescents and adults aged 11–64 years was licensed in the United States (Adacel®, Sanofi Pasteur). 13. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) reviewed evidence and considered the use of Tdap among adults during public meetings held between June 2005 and February 2006. 14. On October 26, 2005, ACIP recommended the routine use of Tdap among adults aged 19–64 years. 15. For adult contacts of infants, ACIP recommended Tdap at an interval as short as two years since the previous Td dose. 16. On February 22, 2006, ACIP recommended Tdap for healthcare personnel, also at an interval as short as two years since the last Td dose. 17. This report summarizes the rationale and recommendations for the use of Tdap among adults in the United States. 18. Recommendations for the use of Tdap among adolescents are discussed elsewhere. 19. During 1934–1943, an annual average of 200,752 pertussis cases and 4,034 pertussis-related deaths were reported in the United States. 20. Although whole-cell pertussis vaccines became available in the 1920s, they were not routinely recommended for children until the 1940s, when they were combined with diphtheria and tetanus toxoids (DTP). 21. The number of reported pertussis cases declined dramatically following the introduction of universal childhood vaccination. 22. Pediatric acellular pertussis vaccines, which are less reactogenic than earlier whole-cell vaccines, were first licensed for use in children in 1991. 23. ACIP recommended replacing all pediatric DTP doses with pediatric DTaP in 1997. 24. In 2005, two Tdap products were licensed for single-dose use in the United States. 25. Boostrix® (GlaxoSmithKline) is licensed for adolescents aged 10–18 years, while Adacel® (Sanofi Pasteur) is licensed for adolescents and adults aged 11–64 years. 26. ACIP recommended that adolescents aged 11–18 years receive a single dose of either Tdap product instead of Td for booster immunization if they have completed the recommended childhood DTP or DTaP series and have not received Td or Tdap. 27. Adacel® is licensed for use in both adults and adolescents. 28. All references to Tdap in this report refer to the Sanofi Pasteur product unless otherwise indicated. 29. Tdap is licensed for one-dose administration and is not intended for subsequent decennial booster doses or wound prophylaxis. 30. 31. No vaccine containing acellular pertussis antigens alone (without tetanus and diphtheria toxoids) is licensed in the United States. 32. Acellular pertussis vaccines combined with tetanus and diphtheria toxoids have been available for adolescents and adults in other countries, including Canada, Australia, and several European nations. 33. The efficacy of an adolescent and adult acellular pertussis vaccine with the same pertussis antigens as Boostrix® was evaluated in a prospective, randomized trial in the United States. 34. In this trial, vaccine efficacy against confirmed pertussis was 92% (95% confidence interval: 32%–99%). 35. 36. Pertussis is an acute respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus. 37. The organism produces toxins that damage respiratory epithelial tissue and have systemic effects, including promoting lymphocytosis. 38. Pertussis is transmitted from person to person through large respiratory droplets generated by coughing or sneezing. 39. The usual incubation period for pertussis is 7–10 days (range: 5–21 days). 40. Patients with pertussis are most infectious during the catarrhal and early paroxysmal phases of illness and can remain infectious for more than six weeks. 41. The infectious period is shorter, usually less than 21 days, among older children and adults with previous vaccination or infection. 42. Patients with pertussis are highly infectious, with attack rates among exposed, non-immune household contacts as high as 80%–90%. 43. Factors affecting the clinical expression of pertussis include age, residual immunity from previous vaccination or infection, and early antibiotic use before cough onset. 44. Antibiotic treatment generally does not modify the course of illness after cough onset but is recommended to prevent transmission of the infection. 45. Vaccination is the most effective strategy for preventing pertussis morbidity. 46. Detailed recommendations on the indications and schedules for antimicrobials are published separately.
